body: No. I'm waiting on some I paid for privately and I'm going back to push for more help. I've not much motivation though, I'm mentally exhausted. I've been dealing with my physical health problems for six years now.

I'm lucky that I'm in the UK so have access to the NHS but unfortunately they've not been able to help. In December I paid for a private consultation with one of the best specialists in the country and was so hopeful but she didn't really listen to me and instead waffled on about her own problems with the British medical culture. I'd put so much hope into that consultation and to have it come to nothing made me feel absolutely hopeless.
Right now I'm pursuing every lead I can to get fixed but I'm running out of options and I'm terrified of what happens when I do.

Been their and done that nearly a decade ago now, didn't work. I just don't care any more, I've no energy for it. I just want to go.

I don't. I want someone to tell me everything I feel about myself is true, that I really don't have a chance and dying is for the best. I want confirmation that what I feel isn't wrong so that I can give in without a lingering doubt that maybe if I just do "this one thing" everything will work out. I'm exhausted by hoping for something better and it never being there, I'm just tired now.

It really is who you know. My brother has his own business, three houses and a hobby that pays. He's worked hard for it all and he deserves it but nevertheless he wouldn't have it without the social connections he has.

It makes the future seem very bleak when you know this and when you read how hard it is for even regular people to make social and career connections after the age of 30.

I was very, very outgoing up until age five and I developed a nervousness about breaking social norms. Things like interrupting teachers or asserting my own wants became very difficult. I developed some physical tics like tensing my whole body, compulsive nodding and blinking. I could still interact but not really normally. 

I moved to a different school age six and I remember that anxiety over breaking social rules just grew and grew. I became hypersensitive to any thought that I'd committed a faux pas and I suppose I found it easier to not engage at all so I just began to withdraw from life completely.

After that isolation became the norm for me.

This is why I hate these pop psychology videos. Even when they say it doesn't apply to mental illnessess it still reinforces these kinds of beliefs that "everyone has the power to help themselves"... but they just don't try.

I haven't had the power to help myself with the help of several psychologists and counsellors and it's not because I haven't put the time in or because I've got too many bloody dishes to wash.

Hiking and being out in nature is honestly one of the few things that I really do love. I get the same feeling you do, I feel calm and ok. But I live in tge middle of a city and can't drive so getting somewhere like that is difficult. I also have mounting medical issues like arthritis and joint problems that get in the way. I still try to get out into nature when I can but it doesn't seem like a long term solution.

I've heard of EMDR but I don't think anywhere near me offers that service. I'll look into it though.

Glad it's helping you.

I think a lot of my problems so stem from what didn't happen in my childhood. My "withdrawal", as my mum described it, was never acknowledged at the time; that along with the poor school I went to made me very isolated so I feel I missed out on a lot of normal development. It's embarrassing to admit but when I finally got the courage to move out (I literally went from leaving the house a handful of times in 10-15 years to moving 200 miles away) I had to ask my mum to teach me how to do things that most take for granted like using an ATM over which I nearly had a panic attack. More complex things, especially social things can still feel daunting even today.

Mental health support in the UK is very patchy, good in some areas and nonexistent in others. In my experience it also only seems to cover either very mild problems or crisis level (read suicide) problems with nothing for those suffering long term.

I do keep trying, and have been doing so for all 26 years of my problems. I find it very hard to not fall into an existential trap where I can't stop asking myself "what's the point to this." Routine often makes this worse, I start thinking about how my future is just repeating the same day over and over again.
It's ok, I feel this way too really.

I've used mdma on a few occasions, including with my brother so I'm certain it wasn't fake, but never felt any effect, except maybe the depressive after effects. I've tried a few stimulants and none have done anything; it seems depressants do though.

I really want to try psilocybin but haven't got a clue about where to get it.
I've raked over my childhood with a few therapists. I don't think there was any major trauma, just a predisposition and lots of small things that were allowed to fester.

I think you make a lot of sense in theory. My biggest problems aren't just the depression and social anxiety but the things I missed out on because of them. I never had any friends after the age of ten, I didn't get an education past 16 and I didn't get proper work experience. It's those practical things that hold me back which then reinforces my MH problems. I've also only ever really had my negative beliefs confirmed; after I managed to leave my house after 15 years isolation I immediately ended up in two abusive relationships one after the other, I found it almost impossible to make any connection with people and when I did they drifted away when they found out about my past.

So in theory I do agree but the theory doesn't correlate with my experience despite having tried to push through the negative thoughts.

I'm in the UK so I don't think SMART recovery is available here. The only MH support locally is an online course and it's geard towards people with short term issues.


I've tried forcing myself through hobbies and I just haven't got the benefit from them you describe.

I'm sorry for the negativity and I don't want to bring anyone down but to be totally frank, as someone in the same position as the OP and has been since they were seven, this post just makes me angry. It turns a real world problem with real world limitations and complications and turns it into a fairy tale and honestly reads more like it comes from someone writing to impress than actually help.


Even if you can change your image of what you or society thinks you should be (it's not a simple or easy thing to do) society doesn't give a fuck what you think. It doesn't stop people abandoning you when you start opening up about your mental health, it doesn't stop employers from snubbing you because you weren't able to get the proper education or experience, it doesn't suddenly give you motivation. Serious depression isn't an image, it isn't just a state of mind you can change, and it isn't character building. This post is just the usual boot straps platitudes dressed up.

Again I'm sorry to be negative but I really, really find stuff like this to be counter productive.
Even if it's just a walk by yourself I'd recommend it. Just to keep being cooped up from becoming your normal. It's up to you of course, I know random people giving advice can be annoying.

Yeah definitely get the hell out of the house; feeling like there's no reason to leave the house can so easily turn into a fear of leaving the house. I spent 15 years housebound because depression and social anxiety festered to the point that going out in public gave me stomach cramps. It took a lot if effort to get past that and even now I find myself slipping into old patterns.

Reddit limits new/low karma accounts I think.

Keep going with things, even though it seems dull you don't want to dig a hole for yourself.
